> Execution traces (line-by-line records of a program's runtime behavior) have emerged as a promising input modality for code language models \citep{chen2025tracepile,ding2024traced,wang2025dcsh,ni2024next}.
> Yet feeding thousands of trace lines to a model can be no better than feeding none: the diagnostic signal drowns in routine execution steps.
> \emph{Which trace components actually carry the signal that matters?}
> 
> Prior work found no single trace representation consistently outperforms others \citep{wang2025dcsh}, but focused on generation-oriented tasks.
> \emph{Verdict prediction}---classifying whether a test passes or fails---offers a cleaner testbed: as binary classification, it isolates the learning signal from generation noise, enabling controlled component ablation.
> As fault detection, the model need not simulate execution, only determine whether something went wrong---and if that signal is concentrated in a small trace subset, information density should matter more than quantity.
> 
> We test this hypothesis through the first systematic component ablation of trace representations for verdict prediction.
> Using 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} and MBPP-sanitized \citep{austin2021program}, we decompose a multi-component trace representation (VOTA: exception events + assertion-point comparisons + loop compression) into individual components across four models spanning 1.5B to 13B parameters and three architecture families: Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B/1.5B-Instruct \citep{qwen2025coder}, CodeLlama-13B-Instruct \citep{roziere2024code}, and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct \citep{deepseek2024coder}.

> This near-perfect accuracy holds from 1.5B to 13B parameters, while the code-only baseline (\texttt{no\_trace}) varies from 72.4\% to 76.5\%.

> Exception events concentrate the runtime's primary fault signal---error type, stack frame, and message---in a compact format (median 150 tokens), while non-exception components (variable states, loop iterations, control flow) record \emph{how} the program ran, not \emph{whether} it failed.

> This density perspective explains three key results: (1)~adding trace information beyond exceptions provides no benefit (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}), because low-density content competes for attention; (2)~a tail-truncation budget sweep reveals a sharp phase transition at ${\sim}$500 tokens (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model}), matching the boundary where diagnostic events dominate; (3)~the SFT advantage over regex concentrates on caught-exception boundary cases, confirming semantic signal extraction (\S\ref{sec:ablation}).

> \paragraph{SFT vs.\ regex: semantic understanding.}

\subsection{Format Marker Ablation}
\label{sec:nomarker}

The \texttt{exception\_only} format includes a \texttt{[No exception data in trace]} marker in all pass-class samples (regex baseline B5 exploits this for 99.33\% accuracy; Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}).
To quantify the marker's contribution, we retrain with all format markers removed (\texttt{nomarker} condition).

Qwen-7B 3-seed mean: 97.65\% $\pm$ 0.96 (seeds 42/123/456: 96.55/98.32/98.07\%), a drop of 2.18pp from \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%).

The marker contribution (${\sim}$2pp) accounts for only ${\sim}$9\% of the total exception lift over \texttt{no\_trace} (24.70pp on 7B).
Exception events thus provide two signal layers that show no degradation at smaller scale: structural markers (${\sim}$2pp, regex-learnable) and semantic exception content (${\sim}$22pp, requiring SFT to distinguish caught from uncaught exceptions).

\subsection{Information Density Decomposition}
\label{sec:density}

The 17.29pp gap between \texttt{full\_trace} (81.76\%) and VOTA (99.05\%, 3-seed mean) decomposes via \texttt{full\_trace\_label\_only} (85.94\%$\pm$1.12, 3 seeds; Table~\ref{tab:density}), which retains the full trace but masks all trace tokens from the loss.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Approximate information density decomposition: gradient dilution (${\sim}$24\%) vs.\ information overload (${\sim}$76\%). \texttt{label\_only} and VOTA are 3-seed means on Qwen-7B.}
\label{tab:density}
\small
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{Acc (\%)} & \textbf{$\Delta$ vs.\ full\_trace} & \textbf{Gap explained} \\
\midrule
full\_trace & 81.76 & --- & --- \\
label\_only & 85.94{\scriptsize$\pm$1.12} & +4.18pp & 24\% \\
VOTA & 99.05{\scriptsize$\pm$0.38} & +17.29pp & 100\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}%
}
\end{table}

Gradient dilution accounts for approximately 24\% of the gap (+4.18pp, 3-seed mean): when the model no longer wastes gradient updates on predicting trace tokens, accuracy improves even with identical input.
The remaining ${\sim}$76\% (+13.11pp) reflects information overload at inference: the model receives thousands of irrelevant trace lines that compete for attention with the diagnostic signal, regardless of loss design.
This asymmetry implies that content selection matters more than loss engineering.
Cross-model evidence supports this: the tail-truncation phase transition at ${\sim}$500 tokens (\S\ref{sec:trace_length}, all four models) coincides with exception traceback length, indicating that retaining diagnostic content is the critical factor.
Cross-scale validation on Qwen-1.5B yields a consistent pattern (17\% gradient dilution, 83\% information overload, 3 seeds), confirming that information overload dominates across model scales.
CodeLlama-13B and DeepSeek-6.7B both exhibit label-only collapse (28.5\% accuracy, collapsing to the minority class), limiting the decomposition to models whose tokenizers preserve sufficient trace structure under the training sequence length.
Error analysis provides direct evidence: all 217 \texttt{full\_trace} errors occur in samples where tokenizer truncation removes diagnostic markers, and among the 61 samples where \texttt{full\_trace} underperforms \texttt{no\_trace}, all exhibit the same truncation pattern---confirming that information overload manifests through a mechanical truncation pathway rather than semantic confusion.
The two factors may interact, and label-only loss simultaneously changes multiple optimization dynamics; the 24\%/76\% attribution is an approximate decomposition (Qwen family, 2 scales, 3 seeds each).

\subsection{Additional Analyses}
\label{sec:additional}

\paragraph{Trace length ablation.}
\label{sec:trace_length}
Varying the head-truncated trace token budget (256--no limit) on Qwen-7B yields accuracy in a narrow 77.2\%--81.8\% band with a non-monotonic pattern: 1024-token prefixes (77.23\%) underperform 512-token prefixes (80.42\%, $p{=}.002$), because mid-length prefixes retain enough irrelevant content to mislead the model while discarding diagnostic events near the trace terminus (Appendix~\ref{sec:trace_length_full}).
This non-monotonicity is specific to head-truncation; under tail-truncation, accuracy increases monotonically for two of three models (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model} in Appendix), with only DeepSeek showing a mild architecture-specific reversal at tail-1024$\to$tail-2048 ($-$1.5pp).

\paragraph{Truncation direction and budget curve.}
Tail-truncation (retaining the last $k$ tokens) dramatically outperforms head-truncation: among the three models with complete data, tail-2048 exceeds head-2048 by 15.5--22.6pp, with the gap widening at smaller scale (Qwen-1.5B: +22.6pp vs.\ Qwen-7B: +15.5pp; Appendix~\ref{sec:trace_length_full}, Table~\ref{tab:head_vs_tail}).

A cross-model budget sweep across four models and three architecture families reveals a phase transition localized between 384 and 512 tail tokens.
At tail-384, all models remain near baseline (73.6--82.9\%, only +1.0--6.5pp over tail-256); the steep jump occurs at 384$\to$512 (+11.0--22.0pp), crossing from near-baseline to near-ceiling (${\sim}$94--98\%).
This localizes the critical threshold to ${\sim}$400--500 tokens, matching the typical exception traceback length (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model}).

1	# Trace Verdict Study
2	
3	Code for "Execution Trace Analysis for Verdict Prediction in Code Assessment" — SFT-based models that leverage execution traces to predict pass/fail verdicts.
4	
5	## Overview
6	
7	This project investigates how different representations of execution traces affect the accuracy of fine-tuned language models in predicting code correctness. We compare multiple trace conditions (full trace, exception-only, no-trace, label-only, etc.) across different base models (Qwen2.5-Coder, DeepSeek-Coder) and evaluate with bootstrap confidence intervals, calibration analysis, and cross-dataset generalization.
8	
9	## Requirements
10	
11	- Python 3.10+
12	- PyTorch 2.0+
13	- transformers
14	- peft
15	- datasets
16	- accelerate
17	- trl
18	- scipy, numpy, matplotlib
19	- wandb (optional, for experiment tracking)
20	
21	Install dependencies:
22	```bash
23	pip install torch transformers peft datasets accelerate trl scipy numpy matplotlib wandb
24	```
25	
26	## Project Structure
27	
28	```
29	├── train/
30	│   ├── train_sft.py              # Main SFT training script
31	│   └── gradient_mask_trainer.py  # Custom trainer with gradient masking
32	├── eval/
33	│   ├── evaluate.py               # Main evaluation script
34	│   ├── bootstrap_compare.py      # Bootstrap CI comparison
35	│   ├── calibration.py            # Calibration analysis
36	│   ├── fewshot_eval.py           # Few-shot baseline evaluation
37	│   ├── fewshot_baseline.py       # Few-shot prompting baseline
38	│   ├── zeroshot_eval.py          # Zero-shot evaluation
39	│   └── ...                       # Additional evaluation scripts
40	├── src/
41	│   ├── vota.py                   # VoTA (Verdict-of-Trace Analysis) core logic
42	│   └── assert_decompose.py       # Assert decomposition utilities
43	├── scripts/
44	│   ├── run_seed_robustness.sh    # Multi-seed training
45	│   ├── regex_baseline.py         # Regex heuristic baseline
46	│   └── ...                       # Additional utility scripts
47	├── analysis/
48	│   ├── token_length_analysis.py  # Token length statistics
49	│   ├── trace_ablation_bootstrap.py # Trace ablation with bootstrap
50	│   ├── clustered_bootstrap.py    # Cluster-robust bootstrap CI
51	│   └── ...                       # Additional analysis scripts
52	└── tests/
53	    └── test_vota.py              # Unit tests for VoTA
54	```
55	
56	## Data Format
57	
58	Training/evaluation data uses JSONL format with the following fields:
59	```json
60	{
61	  "input": "<execution trace or code context>",
62	  "output": "pass" or "fail"
63	}
64	```
65	
66	Data preparation scripts are in `data/` (not included in this repository). Place your prepared data files in `./data/`.
67	
68	## Training
69	
70	Example training command (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B with exception-only traces):
71	
72	```bash
73	python train/train_sft.py \
74	    --condition exception_only \
75	    --model_path ./models/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct \
76	    --train_data ./data/exception_only_train.jsonl \
77	    --eval_data ./data/exception_only_test.jsonl \
78	    --output_dir ./checkpoints/exception_only_seed42 \
79	    --max_steps 500 \
80	    --seed 42 \
81	    --gradient_checkpointing
82	```
83	
84	### Conditions
85	
86	| Condition | Description |
87	|-----------|-------------|
88	| `full_trace` | Complete execution trace |
89	| `exception_only` | Only exception/error information from trace |
90	| `no_trace` | Code + test without trace |
91	| `label_only` | Minimal input (verdict label prediction only) |
92	
93	## Evaluation
94	
95	```bash
96	python eval/evaluate.py \
97	    --condition exception_only \
98	    --model_path ./models/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct \
99	    --checkpoint_dir ./checkpoints/exception_only_seed42/final \
100	    --eval_data ./data/exception_only_test.jsonl \
101	    --output ./checkpoints/exception_only_seed42/final/eval_results.json
102	```
103	
104	## Bootstrap Comparison
105	
106	```bash
107	python eval/bootstrap_compare.py \
108	    --pred_a ./checkpoints/condition_a/final/predictions.jsonl \
109	    --pred_b ./checkpoints/condition_b/final/predictions.jsonl
110	```

# Trace Verdict Study

Code for "Execution Trace Analysis for Verdict Prediction in Code Assessment" — SFT-based models that leverage execution traces to predict pass/fail verdicts.

## Overview

This project investigates how different representations of execution traces affect the accuracy of fine-tuned language models in predicting code correctness. We compare multiple trace conditions (full trace, exception-only, no-trace, label-only, etc.) across different base models (Qwen2.5-Coder, DeepSeek-Coder) and evaluate with bootstrap confidence intervals, calibration analysis, and cross-dataset generalization.

## Requirements

- Python 3.10+
- PyTorch 2.0+
- transformers
- peft
- datasets
- accelerate
- trl
- scipy, numpy, matplotlib
- wandb (optional, for experiment tracking)

Install dependencies:
```bash
pip install torch transformers peft datasets accelerate trl scipy numpy matplotlib wandb
```

## Project Structure

```
├── train/
│   ├── train_sft.py              # Main SFT training script
│   └── gradient_mask_trainer.py  # Custom trainer with gradient masking
├── eval/
│   ├── evaluate.py               # Main evaluation script
│   ├── bootstrap_compare.py      # Bootstrap CI comparison
│   ├── calibration.py            # Calibration analysis
│   ├── fewshot_eval.py           # Few-shot baseline evaluation
│   ├── fewshot_baseline.py       # Few-shot prompting baseline
│   ├── zeroshot_eval.py          # Zero-shot evaluation
│   └── ...                       # Additional evaluation scripts
├── src/
│   ├── vota.py                   # VoTA (Verdict-of-Trace Analysis) core logic
│   └── assert_decompose.py       # Assert decomposition utilities
├── scripts/
│   ├── run_seed_robustness.sh    # Multi-seed training
│   ├── regex_baseline.py         # Regex heuristic baseline
│   └── ...                       # Additional utility scripts
├── analysis/
│   ├── token_length_analysis.py  # Token length statistics
│   ├── trace_ablation_bootstrap.py # Trace ablation with bootstrap
│   ├── clustered_bootstrap.py    # Cluster-robust bootstrap CI
│   └── ...                       # Additional analysis scripts
└── tests/
    └── test_vota.py              # Unit tests for VoTA
```

## Data Format

Training/evaluation data uses JSONL format with the following fields:
```json
{
  "input": "<execution trace or code context>",
  "output": "pass" or "fail"
}
```

Data preparation scripts are in `data/` (not included in this repository). Place your prepared data files in `./data/`.

## Training

Example training command (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B with exception-only traces):

```bash
python train/train_sft.py \
    --condition exception_only \
    --model_path ./models/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct \
    --train_data ./data/exception_only_train.jsonl \
    --eval_data ./data/exception_only_test.jsonl \
    --output_dir ./checkpoints/exception_only_seed42 \
    --max_steps 500 \
    --seed 42 \
    --gradient_checkpointing
```

### Conditions

| Condition | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| `full_trace` | Complete execution trace |
| `exception_only` | Only exception/error information from trace |
| `no_trace` | Code + test without trace |
| `label_only` | Minimal input (verdict label prediction only) |

## Evaluation

```bash
python eval/evaluate.py \
    --condition exception_only \
    --model_path ./models/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct \
    --checkpoint_dir ./checkpoints/exception_only_seed42/final \
    --eval_data ./data/exception_only_test.jsonl \
    --output ./checkpoints/exception_only_seed42/final/eval_results.json
```

## Bootstrap Comparison

```bash
python eval/bootstrap_compare.py \
    --pred_a ./checkpoints/condition_a/final/predictions.jsonl \
    --pred_b ./checkpoints/condition_b/final/predictions.jsonl
```

## License

This code is released for research purposes.
